Mild urinary urgency or discomfort may occur for a short period after the procedure, but symptoms that are severe or not improving should be discussed with the treating team. He should not wait for a routine appointment if warning signs develop. He was advised to keep a copy of the discharge information available and share it with his usual clinicians. He may increase activity as comfort allows, while following any additional instructions provided by the procedural team. If nausea prevents adequate drinking or eating, he should contact a clinician for advice rather than allowing symptoms to continue unchecked. He was encouraged to maintain his usual diabetes-related eating routine as feasible and to discuss any prolonged change in intake with his regular clinician. He should also reconnect with his usual clinician to review recovery and continue management of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. The hospital discharge information should be shared with those clinicians. Follow-up is important even if pain remains improved, because the temporary device requires a clear plan. The transition plan was discussed with him before leaving, with emphasis on hydration as tolerated, gradual return to activity, and prompt attention to fever, worsening pain, vomiting, or inability to pass urine. He was discharged in stable condition for continued recovery at home.
